title: Rosh Hashanah: the shofar
hookLine: the new year opens with a ram's horn, a cry without words

lines: A NEW YEAR WITHOUT A COUNTDOWN.
A CURVED HORN, A SILENT ROOM.
cards: Most new years begin with a countdown and a lot of noise. This one begins in a full synagogue. Someone lifts a curved animal horn to their lips, and the room goes silent.
Then it comes: one long, raw, rising note. Then three broken ones, like sighing. Then a run of short, fast blasts, like sobbing.
Then the long note again. No words at all. That is how Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, opens.

teach.h: A DAY OF BLOWING THE HORN.
teach.b: The horn is called a shofar, usually a ram's horn, hollowed out. It's not really an instrument; it has no keys and plays no tune. The Torah never uses the name Rosh Hashanah for this day.
It calls the first day of the seventh month "a day of blowing the horn unto you." That's the whole description: a day of the horn.
The rabbis later named it the head of the year, and taught that on this day the whole world is judged. There are three sounds.
Tekiah, one long blast. Shevarim, three broken notes.

The rabbis weren't sure exactly what the Torah's teruah sounded like, a groan or a whimper, so they kept both, and a widespread custom is to hear the sounds in many combinations, adding up to a hundred blasts over the day.
The last is the tekiah gedolah, the great blast, held as long as the blower's breath will last. Why a ram's horn? It calls to mind the ram Abraham offered in place of Isaac.
A cow's horn isn't used; the rabbis said it would recall the golden calf. And what does it mean?
Maimonides, the medieval legal scholar and philosopher, said the shofar carries a message even though the Torah gives no reason: wake up, you sleepers, from your sleep. Look at your deeds. Come back.
Others hear a coronation trumpet, or a child crying out to a parent without words. Jewish tradition holds all of these.
On the Sabbath it isn't blown, and in many communities it's sounded every weekday morning in the month before, like an alarm set early.

how: On Rosh Hashanah, a shofar is sounded in the synagogue in patterns of tekiah, shevarim and teruah, traditionally a hundred blasts over the day, except on Shabbat. Many communities also blow it each weekday morning in the month of Elul beforehand.

o: a ram's horn, blown as a cry without words
a silver trumpet once used in the Temple
a festive drum played at the new year

games.q: what's inside the shofar — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah calls this day Rosh Hashanah
the Torah calls it a day of blowing the horn. the name Rosh Hashanah comes from the rabbis.
a cow's horn can't be used as a shofar
the rabbis said it would recall the golden calf.
the shofar is blown on Rosh Hashanah even when it falls on Shabbat
when the holiday falls on Shabbat, the shofar isn't blown.

games.q: you're making a shofar for your synagogue. you have a cow's horn and a ram's horn. which do you use?
o: the cow's horn, it's bigger and louder.
games.why: the ram's horn: it recalls the ram Abraham offered instead of Isaac. a cow's horn is ruled out because it would recall the golden calf.

practice: Take one long breath in and let it out slowly, like a tekiah, then three broken breaths out, like shevarim. Then breathe normally and let one question sound: what have I been asleep to?
A person, a habit, a feeling; there's no need to answer out loud.

wordCard.voice: Shofar. A ram's horn, blown on Rosh Hashanah in long, broken and short blasts: a cry without words that says wake up.

orig.note: Hebrew: a ram's horn, blown on Rosh Hashanah and at the close of Yom Kippur.

carryVoice: Your line: wake up. A cry with no words can still say it. That's day one hundred twenty-three.
